title: A topology-optimisation picture is a load path: reading the project's vine mark
summary: The project's mark is the material layout from a compliance-minimising topology optimisation: a branching structure that carries a distributed load into a single support. Read as a structure, it shows where material is needed; as an emblem, it is a human choice of ink and typography.

media.alt: A dark green branching structure on a pale background: a wide top bar from which several branches run down and inward, merging into a single thick trunk at the bottom, with white voids between the branches.

source.caption: The bare vine mark
group: 14_14_logo_topopt_poster: the converged material field with a scripture quotation and the title line 'SIMP compliance minimization, converged, compliance=10.916' (a video of the optimisation, poster frame)
15_15_vine_mark: the same material field alone on a transparent background, the logo asset (representative)
source.note: Decorative and identity figures. The captions state that the geometry is solver output and the ink colour and typography are a human choice. Only the generic reading is taught here.

read_the_figure.question: Where does the structure put material, and why does it branch?
read_the_figure.axes: No axes. The picture is a two-dimensional design domain: the top edge carries a distributed load, the bottom centre is the support, and darkness is material density (dark is solid, white is void).
look_at: Dark members are the load paths: material is kept where internal force is carried.
The branches merge towards the support, because forces from many points must combine into one reaction.
White voids are regions where material would add weight but little stiffness.
Soft, blurred edges are intermediate densities of the numerical method, or image scaling, not a drawn effect.
read_the_figure.proves: That a compliance-minimising solver, given a distributed load and a single support, produces a branching, tree-like layout. It is an illustration, not evidence of a performance gain.
if_wrong: A symmetric layout from asymmetric loads would suggest an imposed symmetry.
Thick grey areas mean unconverged or filtered densities.
must_check: The load and support positions are stated; here the title and caption describe them in words only.
The compliance value is quoted only for its own problem: 10.916 is not comparable with other figures' numbers.
It is stated what is solver output and what is a human choice.
as_drawn: The poster frame prints compliance 10.916 in its title. It belongs to this problem only.
The symmetric branching is consistent with a symmetric load and a centred support; the figure does not give the mesh or the volume fraction.

terms.meaning: Choosing where to put material in a domain to optimise a performance measure under a material budget.
A density-based method where stiffness scales as density raised to a power greater than one, so intermediate densities are discouraged.
Load times displacement; lower is stiffer.
The route by which a force travels through a structure to the support.

remember: Dark is material, white is void.
Branching appears where many loads must combine into one support.
Compliance numbers belong to their own problem.
Solver output and human styling are different things; say which is which.

steps.title: The objective that makes branches
steps.tex: \min_{\boldsymbol\rho}\ c=\mathbf F^{\mathsf T}\mathbf u\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathbf K(\boldsymbol\rho)\mathbf u=\mathbf F,\ \sum_e v_e\rho_e\le V
steps.note: Under a fixed material budget, the stiffest layout concentrates material along the lines of force; a distributed load into a single support yields a tree. The same problem is treated in the topology-optimisation comparison figures.

worked.title: Why a single support produces a single trunk
worked.problem: A load spread along the top edge is carried to one support point. Why must the cross-section of material grow towards the support?

solution.text: Force balance: the vertical force carried grows as more loads are collected.
For a bar of fixed strength the area needed is proportional to the force.

worked.answer: Each branch carries the load collected so far, so the member widens as branches join, giving the thick trunk at the support.

analyze.q: What would change in the layout if the support were moved from the centre to a corner?
analyze.hint: Where do the load paths have to end?

evaluate.q: Is the mark's compliance number a useful quality statistic? What would you need to compare it with?
evaluate.hint: A baseline layout for the same problem.

create: Redraw the mark with the load arrows along the top edge and the support symbol at the bottom, so the reader can see which forces the branches carry.

checks.q: What do white regions mean in a topology-optimisation picture?
checks.answer: Void: places where the solver decided material adds little stiffness for its weight.

checks.q: Three equal loads of 2 kN merge into one trunk. What load does the trunk carry?
Why do branches merge towards the support?
checks.hint: Where does the force have to go?
checks.answer: All loads must end at the support, so branches collect and combine their forces on the way, which makes the structure converge to a single trunk.

checks.q: Why should an emblem made from solver output still state what was a human choice?
checks.answer: Because the geometry is the solver's, but colour, typography and cropping are decisions. Saying so keeps the claim of 'generated, not drawn' accurate.

checks.q: What would you add so the picture teaches the load path?
checks.answer: Draw the distributed load arrows on the top edge, mark the support at the bottom centre, and colour the members by internal force.
